positions/exclusive-psalmody/oneLine: Because the church must sing only what God has given for worship, congregations should sing the inspired Psalms (and, for some, other scriptural songs), usually unaccompanied, rather than hymns of human composition.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/coreClaims/: The Psalter is God’s divinely inspired hymnbook for his people.
"Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs" (Col 3:16; Eph 5:19) correspond to Greek Psalter titles, not to non-inspired compositions.
Uninspired hymns introduce human doctrine and sentiment into worship.
Instruments belonged to Temple ceremonial and are abolished with it.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/origin: Calvin’s Geneva sang metrical psalms and a few canticles (Genevan Psalter completed 1562); Scottish Presbyterians adopted the Metrical Psalter of 1650 and sang psalms exclusively until the 19th century. Today held by the Reformed Presbyterian (Covenanter) churches, the Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland and others; the Free Church of Scotland ended its exclusive psalmody in 2010.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/proponentsO: Theodore Beza and Clément Marot (Genevan Psalter)
Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America
positions/exclusive-psalmody/strongestAr: If only commanded elements are allowed, the only songs certainly commanded are the inspired Psalms.
The Psalms are Christ’s own prayer book, covering the whole range of human experience.
Singing Scripture guards doctrine and unites congregations across centuries and cultures.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/strongestOb: The New Testament contains new songs to Christ (Phil 2:6–11; Rev 5:9–10), suggesting Christian hymnody.
Singing only Old Testament texts can veil the name of Jesus and the fulfilled gospel (Watts’s objection).
Most Reformed bodies, including Westminster’s own heirs, have judged "hymns and spiritual songs" broader than the Psalter.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/responses/0: Exclusive psalmists reply that the Psalms speak of Christ throughout (Luke 24:44) and are to be sung in the light of their fulfilment.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/responses/1: They argue that New Testament hymn fragments, being inspired, do not license uninspired compositions.
positions/exclusive-psalmody/consequence: Distinctive Scottish, Ulster and American Covenanter worship.
Metrical psalm traditions such as Gaelic psalm "precenting".
Debates in Presbyterian assemblies over hymns from the 19th century to 2010.
positions/acappella-worship/oneLine: The New Testament church sang without instruments, and since Christians are to follow apostolic precedent (or because instruments belonged to the Temple’s ceremonial worship), congregational singing should be unaccompanied.
positions/acappella-worship/coreClaims/0: New Testament worship commands singing (Eph 5:19; Col 3:16), not playing.
positions/acappella-worship/coreClaims/1: Silence of Scripture prohibits rather than permits (Restorationist hermeneutic: command, example, necessary inference).
positions/acappella-worship/coreClaims/2: The early church fathers and the Eastern churches worshipped without instruments for centuries.
positions/acappella-worship/coreClaims/3: The human voice is the instrument God seeks: "making melody in your heart".
positions/acappella-worship/origin: Instruments were not used in early Christian worship (Clement of Alexandria and Chrysostom contrast Christian song with pagan or Temple instruments) and remain absent from Eastern Orthodox services; organs entered the Western church from about the 9th–13th centuries. Calvin and the Reformed removed organs; the principle became defining for Churches of Christ after the 1860–1906 division.
positions/acappella-worship/strongestArg: Historical scholarship (e.g. Ferguson) confirms that early Christian worship was vocal only.
It guards worship from performance and spectacle and fosters strong congregational singing.
It follows a consistent principle of New Testament precedent rather than taste.
positions/acappella-worship/strongestObj: Psalm 150 commands praise with instruments, and Revelation depicts harps in heaven (Rev 5:8).
Silence of Scripture is not a prohibition; Christians use many unmentioned aids (hymnbooks, buildings, pitch pipes).
Making it a test of fellowship divided the Stone-Campbell movement over a matter many see as indifferent.
positions/acappella-worship/responses/0: Advocates reply that the Old Testament instruments belonged to the Levitical system and that heavenly imagery is symbolic.
positions/acappella-worship/responses/1: They distinguish aids to an authorised element (singing) from additions of a new element (playing).
positions/acappella-worship/consequences: The a cappella Churches of Christ (c.1.5 million in the USA; growing in Africa and India).
Strong traditions of four-part congregational singing.
Orthodox and Amish unaccompanied chant and hymnody.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/oneLine: True worship is inward and spiritual; Friends gather in expectant silence without liturgy, sacraments or appointed minister, speaking only when moved by the Spirit of Christ.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/coreClai: God is Spirit and is worshipped in spirit (John 4:24), not tied to forms, places or times.
Christ is present to teach his people himself; every member may minister as led.
Outward sacraments are replaced by inward baptism and communion.
Silence allows the "creaturely" self to be stilled so that the Light can be heard.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/origin: George Fox and the early Friends (from 1652) abandoned "steeple-house" worship; Robert Barclay’s Apology (1676/1678) gave the theological rationale. Programmed (pastoral) worship emerged among American Friends after the 19th-century revivals, and is now the majority form in Kenya and Latin America.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/stronges: It takes seriously Jesus’ teaching that worship is not bound to temple or mountain.
It allows every believer, women included from the start, to minister as the Spirit leads.
It avoids empty formalism and reliance on clergy.
Most Christians argue that Christ commanded outward baptism and the Lord’s Supper.
Without Scripture reading and teaching, meetings can drift into vague spirituality (a criticism made by evangelical Friends).
Silence can become its own fixed form.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/response: Friends reply that inward reality matters more than outward signs, which Jesus fulfilled.
Many meetings include Scripture-informed vocal ministry and value discernment by the gathered meeting.
positions/quaker-silent-worship/conseque: A distinctive tradition of silent worship influencing contemplative practice beyond Quakerism.
Equal ministry of women from the 1650s.
Division between unprogrammed and programmed/evangelical Friends.
positions/revivalist-new-measures/oneLin: Worship services should be designed to bring sinners to decision and believers to renewal, using whatever methods prove effective, since God works through the right use of means.
positions/revivalist-new-measures/coreCl: Revival results from the faithful use of appropriate means, not a miracle beyond human agency (Finney).
The sermon and service should press hearers to immediate decision (anxious bench, altar call).
Forms of worship are pragmatic and may change to reach new audiences.
Lay participation, including women praying aloud in mixed meetings, is encouraged.
positions/revivalist-new-measures/origin: Camp meetings (Cane Ridge, 1801) and Methodist circuit preaching; Charles Finney’s campaigns (1825–35) and Lectures on Revivals (1835); continued by D. L. Moody and Ira Sankey (1870s), Billy Sunday, Billy Graham’s crusades and the seeker-service model of Willow Creek (1975).
positions/revivalist-new-measures/strong: Paul adapted his methods to his audiences to "save some".
The approach reached millions on the American frontier and in cities, especially among the unchurched.
It gave ordinary people, women and African Americans a voice in worship (Hatch).
Nevin and others argue it rests on human technique and emotional pressure rather than God’s means of grace.
Calvinist critics charge that it presupposes a Pelagian-leaning view of human ability (Finney rejected inherited guilt).
It tends to subordinate worship of God to evangelistic results and consumer preference.
positions/revivalist-new-measures/respon: Revivalists answer that God uses human means (preaching itself is one) and that the fruit of transformed lives validates the methods.
Later evangelicals (Graham) combined the altar call with a firmer theology of grace.
positions/revivalist-new-measures/conseq: The altar call and gospel song as fixtures of evangelical worship.
Shaped Pentecostal and megachurch worship styles.
Provoked liturgical and confessional reactions (Mercersburg, Oxford Movement, Lutheran confessionalism).
positions/pentecostal-charismatic-worshi: Pentecostal and charismatic worship
Spirit-led worship
Praise and worship
Charismatic worship
Worship is an encounter with the living God in which the Holy Spirit moves freely through praise, tongues, prophecy, healing and bodily expression, as on the day of Pentecost.
The Spirit’s gifts (1 Cor 12–14) belong in congregational worship today.
Praise is expressed with the whole body: raised hands, clapping, dance, kneeling, falling.
Worship leads into the presence of God, often understood in terms of the tabernacle’s outer court, holy place and holy of holies.
Spontaneity is welcomed, though "decently and in order".
Music is central; local musical idioms are embraced.
Acts 2:1–4
1 Corinthians 12–14
Psalm 22:3 ("inhabitest the praises")
Ephesians 5:18–19

Holiness camp meetings and Black church worship fed the Azusa Street revival (1906), from which Pentecostal worship spread worldwide; the charismatic renewal (from 1960) brought it into historic churches, and the Third Wave/Vineyard (1980s) shaped its music.
Aimee Semple McPherson
Jack Hayford
Judson Cornwall
Darlene Zschech
It mirrors the participatory worship Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 14.
Its growth among the world’s poor and in the Global South suggests it meets deep spiritual and cultural needs.
It recovers bodily, emotional and communal dimensions of biblical worship (Psalms).
Cessationists argue that revelatory gifts ceased and that ecstatic phenomena are not biblically authenticated.
Liturgical critics see emotionalism and a lack of sacramental and doctrinal depth.
Excesses (e.g. "holy laughter", manipulation) have caused pastoral harm.
Pentecostals reply that Scripture regulates the gifts (1 Cor 14:26–40) rather than abolishing them.
Many charismatic Catholics, Anglicans and Lutherans combine Spirit-led praise with liturgy and sacraments.
The fastest-growing style of Christian worship in the 20th–21st centuries.
Major influence on global worship music and on Catholic charismatic renewal.
Debates over discernment of manifestations (Toronto, Brownsville).
positions/contemporary-worship-music/one: Congregational worship should use the musical language of contemporary culture, with band-led sets of simple, singable songs expressing personal devotion to God, so that worship is accessible and authentic.
positions/contemporary-worship-music/cor: "Sing unto the Lord a new song" (Ps 96:1): every generation should write its own songs.
Worship should be intelligible and culturally accessible (1 Cor 14).
Extended musical sets allow worshippers to encounter God personally and emotionally.
Musical style is neutral; content and heart matter.
positions/contemporary-worship-music/ori: The Jesus Movement and Calvary Chapel’s Maranatha! Music (1971), the Vineyard (1980s), Integrity’s Hosanna! Music (1987), the licensing agency CCLI (1988), the UK’s Graham Kendrick and Matt Redman, Australia’s Hillsong (from the 1990s) and US churches such as Bethel and Elevation.
positions/contemporary-worship-music/pro: Keith and Kristyn Getty (modern hymn writers)
positions/contemporary-worship-music/str: Hymns now considered traditional (Watts, Wesley) were contemporary and controversial in their day.
It has drawn young people and the unchurched, and travels easily across cultures and languages.
It fosters wholehearted participation and personal devotion.
Critics argue that lyrics are often theologically thin, repetitive and focused on the self ("me and Jesus").
Performance-style lighting and volume can turn congregations into audiences.
A small number of megachurch publishers dominates global repertoires, raising concerns about commercialism and the theology of their source churches.
positions/contemporary-worship-music/res: Advocates note the "modern hymn" movement and theologically rich songwriting, and argue that simplicity serves participation.
Many churches blend contemporary songs with hymns and liturgy ("blended worship").
positions/contemporary-worship-music/con: Dominant worship style of evangelical and Pentecostal churches worldwide.
The "worship wars" of the 1990s and continuing debates over Hillsong and Bethel.
